title: Rio de Janeiro: Who, Which, Where, Whose

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *que*, *quien*, *donde* and *cuyo* from B1 Unit 5: *que* for people and things, *quien* after a preposition, *donde* for places and *cuyo* for "whose". They let one sentence describe a place in detail, which is what a description of Rio needs: hills, bay, districts. Here they work on Rio de Janeiro.

sections.title: Four relatives at work
rows: Los morros que rodean la bahía forman un anfiteatro natural.
*que* for things: the hills that surround the bay
Los navegantes que llegaron en 1502 creyeron que la bahía era un río.
*que* for people: the sailors who arrived
El Corcovado, donde está el Cristo Redentor, mira sobre la ciudad.
*donde* for a place: where the statue stands
La bahía de Guanabara, cuyas aguas bañan muchas playas, tiene varias islas.
*cuyas* agrees with *aguas*, the thing owned: whose waters

items.spanish: La ciudad donde se instaló la corte portuguesa en 1808 era Río de Janeiro.
items.english: The city where the Portuguese court settled in 1808 was Rio de Janeiro.

items.spanish: El Pan de Azúcar, que se ve desde muchas playas, es uno de sus símbolos.
items.english: Sugarloaf Mountain, which can be seen from many beaches, is one of its symbols.

items.spanish: Hay barrios cuyos vecinos viven en las laderas de los morros.
items.english: There are districts whose residents live on the hillsides.

sections.content: Without commas, the relative clause says which one you mean (*los morros que rodean la bahía*: only those hills). Between commas, it adds extra information about something already clear (*El Corcovado, donde está el Cristo Redentor, ...*). *Cuyo* agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner, and no article comes after it.
